definitions.definition: The Tattvārthasūtra's seven realities — soul, non-soul, inflow, bondage, stopping, shedding, liberation — whose right understanding is right view (TS 1.2, 1.4); the Śvetāmbara canon and Kundakunda count nine categories by adding merit and demerit.
The nine realities (nava tattva): jīva, ajīva, puṇya, pāpa, āsrava, saṃvara, nirjarā, bandha, mokṣa (Navatattvaprakaraṇa; Haribhadra's Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya).

relations.note: Belief in the realities is the content of right view (TS 1.2).

definitions.definition: The universe consists of six eternal, uncreated substances: souls, matter, the medium of motion, the medium of rest, space and time; all but time are 'extended' (astikāya); only matter has form (TS 5.1–5, 5.39).
Some Śvetāmbara authorities treat time only as a mode of the other substances ('time too, according to some', Śv TS 5.38).

relations.note: The substances being eternal and uncreated, there is no creator (TS 5.4).

definitions.definition: A substance possesses qualities (co-present, inseparable, themselves without qualities) and modes (successive states); the becoming of qualities is transformation (TS 5.38, 5.41–42).

name: The triple mark of the existent

definitions.definition: Whatever exists is endowed with origination, cessation and persistence (TS 5.30): permanent as substance, changing as modes — the ontological root of many-sidedness and the Jain answer to both eternalism and momentariness.

relations.note: The triple mark grounds many-sided predication (TS 5.32).

name: Matter, atoms and aggregates

definitions.definition: Matter (pudgala) consists of partless atoms and their aggregates, formed by union and division and bound by degrees of smoothness and roughness; it has touch, taste, smell and colour and takes the forms of sound, light, shadow and bodies; body, speech, mind, breath, pleasure and pain are its services, and karma is a subtle kind of matter (TS 5.19–28, 5.33–37).

members: vargaṇā (classes of matter: e.g. karmic, linguistic, mental)

definitions.definition: A word may refer to a thing by name only, by representation (image), by potentiality (what it was or will be) or by its actual present state; distinguishing these avoids confusion (TS 1.5).
The five knowledges are themselves pramāṇa: sensory and scriptural are indirect, clairvoyance, mind-reading and omniscience direct, because only knowledge by the soul alone is direct (TS 1.9–12).
Akalaṅka's system: direct cognition is conventionally direct (sense-perception) or truly direct; indirect cognition is memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and scripture (Laghīyastraya).
Valid cognition illuminates itself and its object and is free of contradiction (Nyāyāvatāra 1); it is the right ascertainment of an object (Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.1.2).

relations.note: Nyāya and Yoga call sense-perception pratyakṣa; the TS calls it parokṣa since it depends on senses.

definitions.definition: Knowledge is sensory (mati), scriptural (śruta), clairvoyant (avadhi), mind-reading (manaḥparyaya) and omniscient (kevala); the first three can be erroneous in one of wrong view; up to four can coexist, omniscience stands alone (TS 1.9–33).

name: The four stages of sensory cognition

definitions.definition: Sensory cognition proceeds by apprehension, speculation, determination and retention (TS 1.15), each over twelve kinds of object (1.16).

Knowledge of all substances in all their modes (TS 1.29), arising when delusion and then the knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring and obstructive karmas are destroyed (10.1); the soul's own nature fully manifest. Its possibility is argued from the degree-wise diminution of faults (Āptamīmāṃsā 4–5).
In the omniscient, knowledge and perception alternate moment by moment (Jinabhadra); Siddhasena holds them identical (Sanmati kāṇḍa 2).
Omniscient knowledge and perception are simultaneous (Digambara commentators).

relations.note: Both are named 'kevala/kaivalya' final states, but the Jain state is omniscience of all modes by a soul that remains individual; Patañjali's kaivalya is the seer's isolation from prakṛti.
Omniscience precedes final liberation at the end of life (TS 10.1–5).

name: The doctrine of standpoints (nayavāda)

definitions.definition: A thing is known through valid knowledge and standpoints (TS 1.6); the seven standpoints — naigama, saṃgraha, vyavahāra, ṛjusūtra, śabda, samabhirūḍha, evambhūta — each grasp one aspect (1.33); the two root standpoints are substance-oriented and mode-oriented; each taken alone is false, all together right (Sanmati). Every rival doctrine is a standpoint made absolute.
Five standpoints with subdivisions (Śv TS 1.34–35); Mallavādin's wheel of twelve views; Yaśovijaya's refuge in all standpoints.

relations.note: The standpoints are the analytic instrument of many-sidedness.

notes: Source of the ontology's reconciliation principle P2-standpoint.

definitions.definition: Reality is many-sided: a thing is permanent and impermanent, one and many, existent and non-existent, each in a definite respect (TS 5.30–32); every absolute (ekānta) assertion grasps only one side and is refuted (Āptamīmāṃsā). The Jina's word is the union of the partial views (Sanmati 3.69).
The Jain doctrine accepts all standpoints without partisanship (Anyayogavyavacchedikā 30); Haribhadra and Yaśovijaya apply it irenically to other darśanas.

Every predication is qualified by 'syāt' (in some respect); with respect to any attribute a thing admits seven predications: is, is not, is and is not, inexpressible, is and inexpressible, is not and inexpressible, is, is not and inexpressible (Āptamīmāṃsā 14, 104–105); statements presenting the whole belong to pramāṇa, partial ones to naya (Rājavārttika).

name: The ultimate and conventional standpoints (niścaya and vyavahāra)

definitions.definition: Kundakunda's pair: the ultimate (pure) standpoint sees the soul as unbound, one and made of knowledge; the conventional describes it through its relations with karma, body and practice; the conventional is needed to teach the ultimate but is not its real meaning (Samayasāra 8, 11, 14); the wise disciple understands both and becomes impartial (Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 8).

For the Adhyātma movement the ultimate standpoint and self-experience are the heart of the path; one-sided adherence to either standpoint is a wrong view (niścayābhāsa, vyavahārābhāsa) (Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka; Ardhakathānaka).

Haribhadra: in the ultimate sense yoga is the three jewels in the soul, in the conventional sense their causes such as serving the teacher (Yogaśataka 2–4); Yaśovijaya joins knowledge-yoga and action-yoga.

relations.note: Analogous only: both distinguish an ultimate from a conventional account, but the Jain ultimate is the soul's own pure nature, not emptiness; Jain texts would reject identification with the Buddhist ultimate.

definitions.definition: The soul is an eternal, formless, conscious substance marked by cognitive activity (upayoga); agent and enjoyer of its karma; co-extensive with its body, contracting and expanding like a lamp's light; souls are innumerable and each distinct; worldly or liberated (TS 2.8–10, 5.3, 5.16; Dravyasaṃgraha 2).
By the ultimate standpoint the soul is the pure knower, not the doer of material karma; 'the soul is other, matter is other' is the whole of reality (Iṣṭopadeśa 50; Samayasāra 38).

relations.note: Unlike the Sāṃkhya-Yoga puruṣa, the Jain soul is an agent, changes in its modes and is body-sized.

definitions.definition: The defining mark of the soul: its activity of knowing (eight kinds: five knowledges and three erroneous) and perceiving (four kinds: visual, non-visual, clairvoyant, omniscient) (TS 2.8–9).

name: Pure, auspicious and inauspicious cognitive states

definitions.definition: Kundakunda's Pravacanasāra distinguishes the pure state (śuddhopayoga) — the soul resting in itself, cause of liberation — from the auspicious (devotion, vows; cause of merit) and the inauspicious (passion; cause of demerit).

notes: Rests on Pravacanasāra (U34's text); no U35 teaching yet.

name: The five states of the soul (bhāva)

definitions.definition: The soul's states are subsidential, destructional, mixed, rising and inherent, with 2, 9, 18, 21 and 3 divisions (TS 2.1–7); at liberation all cease except perfect right view, knowledge, perception and siddhahood (10.3–4).
Infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy — the soul's own nature, fully manifest when the four destructive karmas are destroyed (cf. TS 2.4, 10.4).

Souls are liberated or worldly; worldly souls are with or without mind, mobile or immobile; one-sensed beings are embodied in earth, water, fire, air and plants; others have two to five senses (TS 2.10–24); the lowest are the nigoda beings sharing one body.

relations.note: The extent of non-violence follows from the extent of life (one-sensed beings included).

name: The ten vitalities (prāṇa) of the embodied soul

definitions.definition: An embodied soul lives by up to ten vitalities: five senses, three powers (mind, speech, body), breath and lifespan; one-sensed beings have four; injury is the severing of these (TS 7.13; Dravyasaṃgraha).
Hemacandra also describes the five winds (prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna) with their seats and colours, but does not make their control a means to liberation (YŚ 5–6).

relations.note: The Jain prāṇas are life-capacities rather than a system of winds to be controlled.

definitions.definition: At birth a soul completes, within an antarmuhūrta, the capacities for taking in matter, body, senses, respiration, speech and mind (Gommaṭasāra and Śvetāmbara karma texts).

Gross, transformable, projectable, fiery and karmic bodies, each subtler than the last; the fiery and karmic bodies are unobstructed and beginninglessly joined to every worldly soul, and carry it between births (TS 2.36–49).

relations.note: Both are layered bodies, but the Jain bodies are material vehicles of the soul, not coverings of an unchanging Self.

definitions.definition: Embodied existence is hellish, animal (including plants and elementary beings), human or divine, according to lifespan and body-making karma; only from the human state is liberation possible (TS 2.6, 8.10).
Birth is by agglutination, from the womb, or by spontaneous arising (gods, hell-beings) (TS 2.31–35), in nine kinds of birth-place.

At death the soul, with only its fiery and karmic bodies, moves along the rows of space-points to its next birth-place, straight in one instant or with up to three bends; for up to three instants it takes in no matter; the liberated soul rises straight up (TS 2.25–30).

relations.note: The Jain transit lasts at most a few instants; there is no extended intermediate existence.

name: Death, lifespan-binding and rebirth in Jainism

definitions.definition: The lifespan karma for the next life is bound once during the present life; at death the soul passes in transit to the destiny so fixed; the lifespans of the spontaneously born and those in their last body cannot be cut short (TS 2.25–30, 2.53, 8.10). The soul-colouring (leśyā) at death is said to accompany rebirth (Śvetāmbara canon, recalled).
Signs foretelling the time of death are described so that the practitioner can prepare (YŚ 5).

name: The kinds of death

definitions.definition: Five kinds of death — 'wise-wise' (of the omniscient), wise (of the ascetic), wise-foolish (of the layman), foolish (of one with right view but no vows) and foolish-foolish (of the wrong-believer); the wise death by renunciation of food is praised (Bhagavatī Ārādhanā).

notes: Classification recalled; Bhagavatī Ārādhanā also lists seventeen kinds of death (not recorded here).

name: Sallekhanā (the final fast)

definitions.definition: At the approach of inevitable death — from calamity, famine, old age or incurable disease — the practitioner gradually gives up food and passions in equanimity, with the teacher's permission and under the care of attending ascetics (TS 7.22; Ratnakaraṇḍa 122; Bhagavatī Ārādhanā). It is vitiated by wishing to live, wishing to die, affection, recalling pleasures and longing for reward (TS 7.37). The texts hold it is not self-killing because it is free of passion (Sarvārthasiddhi 7.22; Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 177–178).
Known as saṃthārā; three forms of the final renunciation of food are distinguished (bhakta-pratyākhyāna, iṅginī, prāyopagamana).

notes: Restricted topic: summary and the texts' own conditions and warnings only; no procedure.

definitions.definition: By inherent nature some souls are capable of liberation and some never will be (TS 2.7); even among the capable, not all will attain it.

name: The state of the liberated (siddha)

definitions.definition: Freed of all karma, the soul rises in one instant to the summit of the universe — like a potter's wheel, a gourd freed of clay, a castor seed and a flame — and stops there for want of the medium of motion; it abides bodiless, in its last body's shape, with perfect right view, knowledge, perception and siddhahood, one among infinitely many (TS 10.3–9).
Haribhadra: the one goal, nirvāṇa, is called by others Sadāśiva, the supreme Brahman, the perfected self and suchness (YDS 129–130).

members: eight qualities (Digambara): samyaktva, jñāna, darśana, vīrya, sūkṣmatva, avagāhana, agurulaghutva, avyābādhatva

definitions.definition: Release from all karma through the absence of the causes of bondage and through shedding (TS 10.2); it follows omniscience and the stopping of all activity; the liberated do not return.
The self conquered by passions is saṃsāra; the same self conquering them is liberation (YŚ 4.5).

Karma is subtle matter drawn in through the soul's activity and bound by its passions, adhering to all its space-points (TS 8.2, 8.24); the soul's passional states are 'psychic karma', the particles 'material karma'.
By the ultimate standpoint the soul is not the doer of material karma; it is the doer only of its own states.

relations.note: Karma here is a material substance, not only a latent impression.

definitions.definition: Knowledge-obscuring (5 subtypes), perception-obscuring (9), feeling (2), deluding (28), lifespan (4), body-making (42, expanded to 93), status (2) and obstructive (5) — 97 (or 148) in all (TS 8.4–13); each has its own causes (TS 6.10–27).

The four destructive (ghātiyā) karmas — knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding, obstructive — obscure the soul's own qualities; their destruction yields omniscience (TS 10.1). The four non-destructive — feeling, lifespan, body-making, status — continue in the living omniscient until death.

Bondage is of nature (which karma), duration (how long), intensity (how strong its fruit) and quantity (how many particles) (TS 8.3); activity determines nature and quantity, passion determines duration and intensity (commentaries).
Wrong view, non-abstinence, carelessness, passion and activity (TS 8.1); they are removed in order through the guṇasthānas.

relations.note: Wrong view ends at stage 4, non-abstinence at 5–6, carelessness at 7, passion at 11/12, activity at 14 (commentaries).

definitions.definition: The activity of body, speech and mind is the channel of inflow; auspicious activity brings merit, inauspicious demerit; with passions it binds lastingly, without passions only transiently (TS 6.1–6).
Because of its passions the soul takes in matter fit for karma: that is bondage (TS 8.2).

The blocking of inflow by the three controls, five carefulnesses, ten virtues, twelve reflections, conquest of the twenty-two hardships and the five conducts (TS 9.1–2); inflow is always to be abandoned and stopping adopted (Vītarāgastotra 19).

The falling away of karma, either after fruition (savipāka) or ahead of time through austerity (avipāka) (TS 8.23, 9.3); shedding increases innumerable-fold at each of ten stages from right view to the Jina (9.45).

Karma is bound, remains (sattā), rises in fruition (udaya), can be prematurely drawn out (udīraṇā), transferred between subtypes (saṅkramaṇa), increased or decreased in duration and intensity (utkarṣaṇa, apakarṣaṇa), subsided (upaśama), fixed (nidhatti) or made unalterable (nikācanā); it is experienced by its nature and then shed (TS 8.21–23; Gommaṭasāra).
Auspicious activity binds merit (pleasant feeling, auspicious lifespan, name and status), inauspicious binds demerit (TS 6.3, 8.25–26).
Merit too binds — a golden fetter; the aim is the pure state beyond both.

name: The passions and their sixteen grades

definitions.definition: Anger, pride, deceit and greed, each in four grades — endless-binding (blocking right view), blocking partial renunciation, blocking full renunciation, and smouldering (blocking perfect conduct) — with nine quasi-passions (TS 8.9).

Six colourings of the soul by passion-tinged activity — black, blue, grey (inauspicious), yellow-red, lotus-pink, white (auspicious) — found in hell-beings, gods and humans in differing degrees (TS 2.6, 3.3, 4.2, 4.22); illustrated by six travellers who would uproot, cut, lop, strip, pick or gather from a fruit tree (Gommaṭasāra Jīvakāṇḍa; the jambū-tree parable).

Purity of view, humility, faultless vows, constant knowledge, fear of saṃsāra, giving and austerity according to capacity, tending ascetics, service, devotion to arhats, teachers, the learned and scripture, the essential duties, promoting the path and love for co-religionists (TS 6.24); Śvetāmbara texts give twenty sthānakas.
Abstention from violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness — in part (small vows) for householders, in full (great vows) for ascetics (TS 7.1–2).
Śvetāmbara ascetics add not eating at night as a sixth vow (Daśavaikālika).

relations.note: Same five names as Patañjali's yamas; Patañjali calls them the great vow when universal (YS 2.31). The Jain vows carry the Jain definitions (e.g. violence as careless severing of vitalities).

name: The twelve vows of the householder

definitions.definition: Five small vows, three supplementary vows and four disciplinary vows (TS 7.20–21 names the seven śīlas: directions, region, purposeless harm, equanimity, holy-day fasting, limiting consumables, sharing with guests); the grouping into guṇa- and śikṣā-vratas differs between authors (Samantabhadra, Kundakunda, Hemacandra).
Guṇavratas: directions, consumables, purposeless harm; śikṣāvratas: sāmāyika, limiting region, pauṣadha, sharing with guests (Śvetāmbara standard, recalled).

name: The eight basic qualities of the householder

definitions.definition: Abstaining from wine, meat and honey with the five small vows (Samantabhadra), or with the five udumbara fruits (later authors).

name: The twenty-five contemplations supporting the vows

definitions.definition: Five contemplations for each vow steady it (TS 7.3–8), with the reflections on the harm and suffering of the sins (7.9–10) and on world and body for dread and detachment (7.12).

Friendliness toward all beings, joy toward the more virtuous, compassion toward the afflicted and impartiality toward the unruly (TS 7.11); Hemacandra makes them supports of meditation (YŚ 4.117–122); recited daily in Amitagati's Sāmāyikapāṭha.

relations.note: Same four attitudes as Yoga Sūtra 1.33, with differing objects (YS: the happy, the suffering, the meritorious, the demeritorious). Graded partial.
Closely parallel to the Buddhist brahmavihāras (mettā, muditā, karuṇā, upekkhā); graded partial.

name: Non-violence in Jainism

definitions.definition: Violence is the severing of vitalities through careless, passion-driven activity (TS 7.13); life pervades earth, water, fire, air and plants (2.13); souls support one another (5.21). Inwardly, non-violence is the non-arising of passion and violence its arising; the other sins are forms of violence (Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 42, 44). Non-violence is called the supreme Brahman (Svayambhūstotra).
Material and psychic violence (dravya- and bhāva-hiṃsā) are distinguished; psychic violence is the root.

members: saṅkalpī / ārambhī / udyogī / virodhī hiṃsā (lay classification)

name: The three controls and five carefulnesses

definitions.definition: Proper restraint of mind, speech and body, and care in walking, speaking, seeking alms, handling objects and excreting (TS 9.4–5); together the eight 'mothers of the doctrine' (Uttarādhyayana 24).

Supreme forbearance, humility, straightforwardness, purity, truth, restraint, austerity, renunciation, non-possession and celibacy (TS 9.6); celebrated in the Digambara Daśalakṣaṇa festival; dharma is also the nature of a thing, the three jewels and the protection of beings (Kārttikeyānuprekṣā 478).

Contemplation of impermanence, no refuge, the round of births, aloneness, otherness of self and body, impurity of the body, inflow, stopping, shedding, the universe, the rarity of enlightenment and the well-taught dharma (TS 9.7); the ladder to meditation (Jñānārṇava); subject of Kundakunda's and Kārttikeya's anuprekṣā poems.

Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, insect bites, nakedness, discontent, women, wandering, sitting, lying, abuse, injury, begging, not obtaining, illness, grass-pricks, dirt, honour, intelligence, ignorance and lack of vision, to be endured for the path and for shedding (TS 9.8–9); eleven are said to occur in the Jina (9.11), a sūtra read differently by the two sects.
Equanimity, re-initiation, purification by special austerity, subtle passion and perfect conduct (TS 9.18), rising with the guṇasthānas.

Six external — fasting, eating less, limiting the alms-round, giving up tasty food, lonely lodging, bodily mortification — and six internal — expiation, humility, service, study, abandonment, meditation (TS 9.19–20); austerity both stops and sheds karma (9.3).
The Śvetāmbara list has saṃlīnatā (withdrawal) for lonely lodging and places meditation before abandonment (Uttarādhyayana 30).

Meditation is fixing the mind on one object for up to a muhūrta (TS 9.27); it is sorrowful (four kinds), cruel (four kinds), virtuous (examining the command, harm, fruition and structure) and pure (four stages: with multiplicity, reasoning and shifting; with unity and reasoning; subtle activity; ceased activity); only the last two lead to liberation (9.28–44).
A steady mind is dhyāna, a moving one is citta (Dhyānaśataka 2).

relations.note: TS 9.41–44 use vitarka and vīcāra but define them as scriptural cognition and shifting among object, word and activity — not Patañjali's gross/subtle object-absorptions.

definitions.definition: Equanimity (sāmāyika), praise of the twenty-four Jinas, salutation of the teacher, repentance (pratikramaṇa), abandonment of the body (kāyotsarga) and renunciation (pratyākhyāna) — daily obligations of ascetics and observant laity.
For householders the Digambaras also teach six daily duties: worship, attendance on the teacher, study, restraint, austerity and giving.

name: The eleven stages of the householder (pratimā)

definitions.definition: Right view, vows, equanimity, holy-day fasting, giving up living food, not eating at night, celibacy, giving up undertakings, giving up possessions, not approving household acts, not accepting food prepared for oneself (Ratnakaraṇḍa).

Śvetāmbara list (Upāsakadaśā tradition): view, vow, sāmāyika, pauṣadha, kāyotsarga, celibacy, giving up living food, giving up undertakings, not employing others, not accepting prepared food, living like a monk (recalled).

name: The five kinds of unattached ascetic

definitions.definition: Pulāka, bakuśa, kuśīla, nirgrantha and snātaka, distinguished by restraint, learning, transgression, tīrtha, outer sign, leśyā, rebirth and stage (TS 9.46–47).

name: The fourteen stages of quality (guṇasthāna)

definitions.definition: Fourteen stages of the soul's purification: wrong view, the taste [of falling], mixed, right view without vows, partial restraint, careless restraint, careful restraint, unprecedented, non-returning gross passion, subtle passion, subsided delusion, destroyed delusion, omniscient with activity, omniscient without activity (Sarvārthasiddhi 1.8; Gommaṭasāra); the Tattvārthasūtra itself gives a ten-stage series of increasing shedding (9.45).
Banārsīdās added a chapter on the guṇasthānas to the Samayasāra Nāṭaka so that the knower of the self also knows the stages of conduct.

notes: The path map itself is pth:jain-fourteen-gunasthanas (owned by U51).

name: The three processes and the breaking of the knot

definitions.definition: Before right view first arises the soul passes through three processes of purification — the ordinary, the unprecedented and the non-returning — which break the dense knot (granthi) of attachment and aversion; right view then arises (karma literature; Haribhadra places the knot's breaking at the sthirā view).

Conviction in the realities (TS 1.2), arising spontaneously or by instruction (1.3); its transgressions are doubt, desire, disgust, praise and acquaintance of wrong-believers (7.23); its eight limbs, three kinds (subsidential, mixed, destructional) and five signs (calm, longing for release, detachment, compassion, affirmation).
Faith in the true deity, scripture and teacher, free of three follies and eight prides, with eight limbs (Ratnakaraṇḍa 4).
To regard the true god as god, the true teacher as teacher and pure dharma as dharma (YŚ 2.2).
The soul that takes refuge in the real (the pure self) is of right view (Samayasāra 11).

name: The three selves: outer, inner, supreme

definitions.definition: The self in all embodied beings is outer (identified with the body), inner (discerning itself) or supreme (utterly pure); by means of the inner one attains the supreme and abandons the outer (Samādhitantra 4–5; Paramātmaprakāśa; YŚ 12).
Who the supreme self is, that am I (Yogasāra 22) — every soul's own nature is the paramātman.

relations.note: Commentators place the outer self in stages 1–3, the inner self in 4–12, the supreme self in 13–14 and the Siddha.

definitions.definition: Knowing the self as other than body, karma and passion: 'the soul is other, matter is other' (Iṣṭopadeśa 50); all who are liberated are liberated by it, all who are bound are bound by its absence (Samayasāra-kalaśa 131).
The central practice of the Adhyātma path, rendered in the Samayasāra Nāṭaka.

relations.note: Parallel discrimination of seer and seen in Yoga, but the Jain knower is an agent with changing modes.

definitions.definition: Mitrā, tārā, balā, dīprā, sthirā, kāntā, prabhā, parā (YDS 13), with light like straw-fire, cow-dung fire, wood fire, lamp, gem, star, sun and moon (15), correlated with the eight limbs (yama … samādhi), the removal of eight faults (fatigue, anxiety, distraction, agitation, confusion, delight in other, pain, attachment) and the rise of eight qualities (non-aversion, desire to know, desire to hear, hearing, understanding, reflection, right apprehension, right practice) (16); the first four are unstable and precede the breaking of the knot, the last four are stable.

relations.note: Haribhadra's own correlation of each view with one of Patañjali's eight limbs (YDS 16).
Sthirā (right view after the knot is broken) corresponds to the fourth guṇasthāna; the first four views precede it (commentarial).

name: Yoga by desire, by scripture and by capacity

definitions.definition: Icchā-yoga (wish with carelessness), śāstra-yoga (diligent practice according to scripture) and sāmarthya-yoga (by capacity, beyond scripture), the last twofold — renunciation of dharmas and renunciation of yoga (YDS).

name: The five yogas of the Yogabindu

definitions.definition: Adhyātma, bhāvanā, dhyāna, samatā and vṛttisaṃkṣaya, each better than the last because it joins the soul to liberation (Yogabindu 31).

relations.note: Vṛttisaṃkṣaya echoes Patañjali's cessation of vṛttis but denotes the cessation of the soul's karmically-born activities leading to omniscience.

name: The five yogas of the Yogaviṃśikā

definitions.definition: Posture, sound, meaning, support and the supportless — the first two action-yoga, the last three knowledge-yoga — each in four grades (desire, practice, steadiness, perfection) (Yogaviṃśikā 2), culminating in meditation on the formless Siddha.

name: The four kinds of religious performance

definitions.definition: Performance from affection (prīti), from devotion (bhakti), from scripture (vacana) and without attachment (asaṅga) (Ṣoḍaśaka; YDS on asaṅga in the prabhā view).

name: The five kinds of performance (poison to nectar)

definitions.definition: Religious acts done for this-worldly reward (poison), for heavenly reward (venom), mechanically (non-performance), as a step toward the true (its cause) and with understanding and longing for release (nectar); only the last two count (Yogabindu).

Gotra-yogins (born in the family of yogins), kula-yogins (born with the yogin's dharma), pravṛttacakra-yogins (in whom the wheel of practice turns) and niṣpanna-yogins (the accomplished); the teaching is for the second and third (YDS).

Only a soul in its last cycle (caramāvarta), no longer binding karma of maximum intensity (apunarbandhaka), who performs the preliminaries (pūrvasevā) — worship of teachers and gods, good conduct, austerity, non-aversion to liberation — is fit for yoga (Yogabindu; Yogaviṃśikā).
Detachment born of suffering, born of delusion, and born of knowledge — only the third is true (Adhyātmasāra, following Haribhadra).

The embodied (piṇḍastha, with five concentrations), the word-based (padastha, on mantras and letters), the form-based (rūpastha, on the Arhat) and the formless (rūpātīta, on the Siddha) — in Śubhacandra's Jñānārṇava and Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra 7–10.

name: The five concentrations of embodied meditation

definitions.definition: Earth (a lotus in an ocean of milk), fire (the syllable arhaṃ burning the lotus of the eight karmas and the body), wind (scattering the ashes), water (washing them away) and the essential (seeing oneself as the pure Siddha) (YŚ 7; Jñānārṇava).
Scattered, coming-and-going, clinging and dissolved, with increasing steadiness and bliss; stillness comes from indifference (audāsīnya), not force, culminating in the no-mind state (YŚ 12).

relations.note: Analogous graded states of mind to Vyāsa's five bhūmis (kṣipta … niruddha); the word vikṣipta is shared.

definitions.definition: Through austerity and the destruction-cum-subsidence of karma ascetics may gain powers — the transformable, fiery and projectable bodies, clairvoyance and mind-reading, healing touch, sky-walking and others (TS 1.21–25, 2.47–49); outward wonders do not prove a teacher's greatness (Āptamīmāṃsā 1), and to use or seek them is carelessness.
Hemacandra describes entering another body only as a wonder useless for liberation (YŚ 6.1); Śubhacandra warns against pursuing powers through breath-control.

relations.note: Both traditions treat powers as distractions from liberation.

definitions.definition: The living omniscient (13th stage) has destroyed the four destructive karmas but keeps the four others; he teaches, moves and at the end may equalise his remaining karmas by expanding his soul through the universe (kevali-samudghāta) before liberation.
The kevalin does not eat, suffer hunger or disease; the eleven hardships of TS 9.11 are figurative (Sarvārthasiddhi); his knowledge and perception are simultaneous.
The kevalin takes food, as the scriptures show of Mahāvīra; knowledge and perception alternate (Jinabhadra) or are identical (Siddhasena).

Arhats (embodied omniscients), Siddhas (liberated), Ācāryas (heads of orders), Upādhyāyas (teachers) and Sādhus (ascetics), honoured in the Namaskāra mantra; together they have 108 qualities (12 + 8 + 36 + 25 + 27). The Jina is worshipped as the model of qualities to be attained, not as a giver of grace (Sarvārthasiddhi maṅgala).

name: Jain mantra and its practice

definitions.definition: The Namaskāra mantra is held eternal and the essence of the scriptures; its shorter forms (16, 6, 5, 4, 2, 1 syllables — e.g. 'a-si-ā-u-sā', 'arhaṃ', 'oṃ' analysed as the five initials) are recited and meditated on by the teacher's instruction (Dravyasaṃgraha 49; YŚ 8). Word-based meditation places letters on lotuses in the body. Protective hymns (Uvasaggaharaṃ, Bhaktāmara, Kalyāṇamandira, Ṛṣimaṇḍala) are recited with associated yantras and mantras.
The Sūrimantra, given orally to ācāryas at installation, and the Vardhamāna-vidyā; worship of the Siddhacakra (nine padas).
Mantra manuals of the goddesses Padmāvatī and Jvālāmālinī (Malliṣeṇa, Indranandi) for protection and worldly ends; the Jñānārṇava condemns using mantra and meditation to harm others.

notes: Restricted material (rites for worldly ends, secret mantras): summary only.

definitions.definition: Sound is a mode of matter (TS 5.24), not eternal; speech is produced from the linguistic class of matter; scripture is śruta-jñāna grounded in the omniscient's teaching; the Tīrthaṅkara's divine sound (divyadhvani) is understood by all beings in their own tongues. Words refer by name, representation, potentiality and actuality (TS 1.5).

relations.note: Against the Mīmāṃsā doctrine of eternal sound and an authorless Veda.

name: Teacher, lineage and transmission in Jainism

definitions.definition: The teaching descends from the omniscient Tīrthaṅkara through the gaṇadharas and the lineage of ācāryas; initiation (dīkṣā) with hair-plucking and the great vows; study under the teacher (vācanā); confession and expiation before the teacher; the teacher adapts instruction to the student; the ācārya receives the secret Sūrimantra at installation (Śvetāmbara).

Haribhadra: conventional yoga is serving the teacher and hearing scripture according to capacity (Yogaśataka 3–4); Hemacandra adds what is 'established by experience' to what was learned from scripture and teacher (YŚ 12.1).

name: The marks of the true teacher and how to test a teacher

definitions.definition: The true deity must be faultless, omniscient and the teacher of scripture (Ratnakaraṇḍa 5); outward miracles prove nothing (Āptamīmāṃsā 1); only one whose speech agrees with reason and scripture is trustworthy (Āptamīmāṃsā 6).

Śrīmad Rājacandra's marks of the sadguru: self-knowledge, equal vision, acting only as karma unfolds, unprecedented speech, supreme scriptural knowledge (Ātmasiddhi 10); the sectarian (matārthī) mistakes outward signs for the teacher (Ātmasiddhi 24–33).

name: The six fundamentals (ṣaṭpada) of Śrīmad Rājacandra

definitions.definition: The soul exists; it is eternal; it is the doer of its karma; it is the enjoyer; liberation exists; there is a means to liberation (Ātmasiddhi 43), each defended against a doubter.
Digambara literature is classed as narrative (prathamānuyoga), cosmology and karma (karaṇānuyoga), conduct (caraṇānuyoga) and substances (dravyānuyoga) (Ratnakaraṇḍa 43–46).

The universe (loka) is finite world-space within infinite empty non-world, uncreated and beginningless, shaped like a man standing with arms akimbo, fourteen rajju high: the seven hells below, the disc of the middle world at the waist, the heavens above, and the abode of the liberated at the crown; mobile beings live only in the central channel (trasa-nāḍī) (TS 3–4, 5.12, 10.5–8; Tiloyapaṇṇatti; Lokaprakāśa).

Seven earths one below another — Ratnaprabhā to Mahātamaḥprabhā — with 8.4 million hells, where beings suffer by their own leśyā, from one another and (in the first three) from the asuras, for up to 1–33 ocean-measures (TS 3.1–6).

Concentric continents and oceans, each double the last, around round Jambūdvīpa with Meru at its navel; its seven regions (Bharata … Airāvata) divided by six ranges; humans live only within the Mānuṣottara range (2.5 continents); lands of action (Bharata, Airāvata, Videha) and lands of enjoyment (TS 3.7–39).

Residential, peripatetic, luminous and celestial-vehicle gods (TS 4.1–42); the higher excel in lifespan and purity but have less movement, possession and pride; gods cannot take vows and must be reborn human to be liberated.

Time is beginningless; in Bharata and Airāvata a descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī) and an ascending one (utsarpiṇī) of six periods each follow one another endlessly; twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras appear in the third and fourth periods; we live in the fifth period of the descending half (TS 3.27–28). Durations are measured in pit- and ocean-measures down to the instant (samaya).

relations.note: A cyclic scheme of decline and ascent like the four yugas, but with six periods in each half and no creation or dissolution of the world.

name: The Jain denial of a creator

definitions.definition: The universe of eternal substances is uncreated and beginningless; a creator-God is refuted — where was he before, why would a perfect being create, an unembodied maker cannot act (Ādipurāṇa 4; Āptaparīkṣā; Anyayogavyavacchedikā 6); the omniscient Jina is worshipped but does not create or intervene.
Haribhadra reinterprets 'Īśvara' as the soul capable of perfection and each soul as the 'maker' of its own condition (Śāstravārtāsamuccaya 3).

name: Jain views of the other darśanas

definitions.definition: Every rival doctrine is a standpoint taken as absolute (Sanmati 3.47); the Jina's word is the union of the partial views (Sanmati 3.69); the Jain doctrine alone, accepting all standpoints, is not partisan (Anyayogavyavacchedikā 30). Polemical works refute other schools; doxographies present them without polemic (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya).

Haribhadra: no partiality for Mahāvīra, no hatred for Kapila — accept whatever is reasoned (Lokatattvanirṇaya 38); the goal is one under many names (YDS 129–130); Ānandaghana: the six darśanas are the limbs of the Jina (Covīsī 21).

notes: Relevant to principles P2 and P3; the Jain tradition does not thereby accept that the other darśanas are equally true.

definitions.definition: Ānandaghana sings the Jina as the soul's only beloved and husband, a love without beginning or end (Covīsī 1), and the path as hidden to reason and quarrel but open to experience (Covīsī 2); devotion to the Jina is devotion to the soul's own perfected nature.
Banārsīdās and later Hindi Adhyātma poets (Dyānatrāy, Bhūdhardās) write devotional padas addressed to the self and the Jina.

Right view, right knowledge and right conduct together are the path to liberation (TS 1.1); when a later one is present the earlier ones are necessarily present (Tattvārthabhāṣya 1.1); knowledge without conduct and conduct without knowledge are both useless, like the lame and the blind in a burning forest (Rājavārttika 1.1).
In the ultimate sense the three jewels are the self itself — the self knowing, seeing and abiding in the self (Kundakunda; YŚ 4.2).
Yoga is the three jewels (YŚ 1.15; Yogaśataka 2).

relations.note: Both are threefold paths, but the Jain triad begins with right view of the realities and makes conduct the culminating member; not an equivalence.
